fields.definition: A moduli space is this vague term that describe the set of a certain class objects you want to classify with some structure of a space.
fields.Example:
[[a6fda3d0-9c7a-4775-9331-53d618f5c6e0|Example (Moduli of conics in $\mathbb P^2$)]]
[[a37887f5-925c-4820-9fa2-50ef14b20d11|Example (Moduli space of line bundles)]]

fields.Question: How many conics in $\mathbb P^2$ go through 5 generic points?
fields.answer:
You may solve this question by first changing coordinates, and assume 4 of the 5 points are fixed, then solve specific equations, but this is not the right way.

The best method is to look at the collection of conics in $\mathbb P^2$, they are given by equations
\[a_1x^2+a_2y^2+\dots+a_6yz=0\]
up to scaling of $a_1,\dots,a_6$, meaning each conic identify with a point in $\mathbb P^5$. We say $\mathbb P^5$ is a moduli space of conics in $\mathbb P^2$.

With some intersection theory, you can equate passing through 5 points as satisfying 5 general linear equations in $\mathbb P^5$, which gives the answer 1.
fields.Note: Here the conics come with their embeddings in a fixed $\mathbb P^2$. [[Embd|Forgetting the embedding gives a different moduli problem]].

fields.Question: Is there a scheme $\mathcal M$ such that maps $X\to\mathcal M$ correspond naturally to isomorphism classes of line bundles on $X$?
fields.answer:
Suppose there is. Take $X=\mathbb P^1$ and let $f_0,f_1:\mathbb P^1\to\mathcal M$ correspond to $\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal O(1)$.

Cover $\mathbb P^1$ by its two usual affine charts $U_0,U_1\cong\mathbb A^1$. Both line bundles restrict to the trivial line bundle on either chart:
$$\mathcal O|_{U_j}\cong\mathcal O(1)|_{U_j}\cong\mathcal O_{U_j}.$$
By naturality, $f_0|_{U_j}=f_1|_{U_j}$ for $j=0,1$. Since [[Locl|morphisms of schemes are determined locally]], we get $f_0=f_1$. This would imply $\mathcal O\cong\mathcal O(1)$, which is false: their degrees are $0$ and $1$.

So the functor of isomorphism classes of line bundles cannot be represented by a scheme.
fields.Note: What went wrong? We kept the fact that the bundles are locally isomorphic, but lost the isomorphisms used to compare and glue them. [[Stki|Remembering those isomorphisms]] leads us toward stacks.
fields.Example: [[Lsec|Example (Projective space and line bundles with sections)]]

fields.objectives: We saw what $\'\text{e}$tale maps are. Let's see some properties and define $\'\text{e}$tale sites.

fields.definition:
$f:X\to Y$ is $\emph{quasi-finite}$ if for all $y\in Y$ the fiber 
\[X_y:=X\times_Y\mathrm{Spec}k(y)\]
is finite.

it is $\emph{locally quasi-finite}$ if for all $x\in X$ there exists $x\in U$ open such that $f|_U$ is quasi-finite.

fields.text:
The map 
$$\coprod_{i=1}^\infty\mathrm{Spec}k\to\mathrm{Spec}k$$
is locally quasi-finite but not quasi-finite.

fields.statement: $f:X\to Y$ is $\'\text{e}$tale if and only if it is smooth and locally quasi-finite.

$f:X\to Y$ is $\'\text{e}$tale if and only if for all $x\in X$,there exists $x\in U$ open affine, such that, there exists $V\subseteq Y$ open affine with $f(U)\subseteq V$ such that $f|_U$ is standard etale.

fields.Note: What does this mean? How should we understand this? Even Serre wasn't completely sure: we just somewhat know it is the right thing to look at.

fields.definition: $f:X\to Y$ is $\emph{flat}$ if for all $x\in X$, $\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}\to \mathcal O_{X,x}$ is [[4e97857e-ae16-4e8f-bd2a-56a25baebd34|flat]].
fields.Example:
Flatness is supposed to be the magic term to mean things vary continuously.

[[d9f4b261-af3f-4287-b879-65280526034a|Example (Non-flat morphism)]]

fields.text: $R$ is PID, then $M$ is a flat $R$-module if and only if $M$ is torsion free.

Let $X\to\mathbb A^1_t$ be the family $\mathrm{Spec}[t][x]/(tx)$. 
If $t\neq 0$, the fiber is a point $x=0$. If $t=0$, the fiber is all of $\mathbb A^1_x$.

fields.hypotheses: $f:X\to Y$ is proper and flat of finite presentation, with nonempty fibers. $Y$ is connected.
fields.Reference: [Stacks Project, Lemma 37.30.6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0D4J): the fiber-dimension function is locally constant, hence constant on a connected base.

fields.hypotheses:
$f:X\to Y$ with constant fiber dimension.
$Y$ is smooth.
$X$ is Cohen-Macauley. [another mysterious condition!]

fields.definition:
$\mathrm{\'et}(X)$ is the site where 
\begin{itemize}
\item objects are $\'\text{e}$tale morphisms $Y\to X$
\item morphisms are morphisms over $X$ (necessarily $\'\text{e}$tale).
\end{itemize}
$\mathrm{Cov}(Y\to X)$ consists of 
\[\{Y_i\to Y\}_{i\in I}\]
such that $\coprod_i Y_i\to Y$ is surjective.

fields.text:
Consider $\mathrm{\'et}(\mathrm{Spec}K)$.
The objects are $\coprod \mathrm{Spec}L_i\to \mathrm{Spec} K$ for $L_i$ finite and separable.
Therefore $\mathrm{Spec} \mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)\to \mathrm{Spec}\mathbb Q$ is a covering.

fields.definition:
$\mathrm{\'Et}(X)$ is the site of category $\mathrm{Sch}_X$ where
$\mathrm{Cov}(Y\to X)$ consists of 
\[\{Y_i\xrightarrow{\mathrm{\'et}} Y\}_{i\in I}\]
such that $\coprod_i Y_i\to Y$ is surjective.
A $\emph{topos}$ $T$ is a category equivalent to sheaves on a site.

fields.setting: $U,Y$ are schemes and $U=\bigcup_i U_i$ is an open cover.
fields.statement: If $h,h':U\to Y$ satisfy $h|_{U_i}=h'|_{U_i}$ for every $i$, then $h=h'$.
fields.Example: This is why the local equality of maps in the [[a37887f5-925c-4820-9fa2-50ef14b20d11|line bundle example]] forces equality globally.

fields.text:
For each scheme $X$, keep a category whose objects are line bundles on $X$ and whose morphisms are isomorphisms of line bundles.

Now two objects can be isomorphic without being equal, and the isomorphism itself is part of the data. When we glue local line bundles, the chosen isomorphisms on overlaps must be remembered and must agree on triple overlaps.

A scheme gives a set $\operatorname{Hom}(X,\mathcal M)$. For a stack, the corresponding collection has the structure of a category, so it can retain these isomorphisms. This is the motivation for thinking of stacks as a generalization of sheaves using categories.

cards.title: Example (Projective space and line bundles with sections)

fields.Question: Why does the line bundle example not contradict the fact that $\mathbb P^n$ is a scheme?
fields.answer:
A map $f:X\to\mathbb P^n$ remembers more than a line bundle. It gives
$$L=f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(1)$$
together with the pulled-back coordinate sections $s_0,\ldots,s_n\in\Gamma(X,L)$, which generate $L$ everywhere.

Conversely, a line bundle $L$ with $n+1$ generating sections defines a map to $\mathbb P^n$. On the open set where $s_i$ generates $L$, its coordinates are the regular functions $s_j/s_i$. These local maps agree on overlaps.

Thus maps to $\mathbb P^n$ correspond to isomorphism classes of pairs $(L,(s_0,\ldots,s_n))$ with
$$\mathcal O_X^{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow L.$$
An isomorphism of pairs must carry each $s_i$ to the corresponding section.
fields.Note: The sections have no common zero. Forgetting them leaves the [[a37887f5-925c-4820-9fa2-50ef14b20d11|moduli problem of line bundles]], which is not represented by a scheme.

fields.text:
The [[a6fda3d0-9c7a-4775-9331-53d618f5c6e0|space $\mathbb P^5$ of conics]] classifies conics inside a fixed $\mathbb P^2$. We remember the inclusion $i:C\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^2$, not just the abstract curve $C$.

The embedding gives the line bundle $i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)$ and the three pulled-back coordinate sections. This is the extra data in the [[Lsec|projective-space interpretation]].

An automorphism $\varphi:C\to C$ compatible with the fixed embedding satisfies $i\circ\varphi=i$, and therefore $\varphi=\mathrm{id}_C$. Abstract curves can have nontrivial automorphisms; forgetting the embedding changes the problem.
fields.Note: Generating sections of a line bundle give a morphism to projective space. For an embedding, those sections must give a closed immersion; an arbitrary generated or ample line bundle does not by itself specify an embedding.

fields.definition:
A presheaf $\mathcal F$ consists of a set $\mathcal F(U)$ for each open subset $U\subseteq X$, and a restriction map
$$\rho_U^V:\mathcal F(V)\to\mathcal F(U)$$
for every inclusion $U\subseteq V$.

These maps satisfy
$$\rho_W^V\circ\rho_V^U=\rho_W^U\quad(W\subseteq V\subseteq U),\qquad\rho_U^U=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal F(U)}.$$
So restricting in stages is the same as restricting directly, and restricting to the same open set does nothing.
fields.Note:
Let $\mathrm{Open}_X$ be the category of open subsets of $X$, with inclusions as morphisms. The same data form a functor
$$\mathcal F:\mathrm{Open}_X^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Sets}.$$
This is a special case of a [[Pshc|presheaf on a category]].

fields.definition:
A presheaf on $\mathcal C$ is a functor
$$\mathcal F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Sets}.$$
Thus an object $U$ gives a set $\mathcal F(U)$, and a morphism $u:V\to U$ gives a map in the other direction,
$$\mathcal F(u):\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F(V).$$
For $v:W\to V$, functoriality means
$$\mathcal F(u\circ v)=\mathcal F(v)\circ\mathcal F(u),\qquad\mathcal F(\mathrm{id}_U)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal F(U)}.$$
fields.Example:
[[Psht|Presheaves on a topological space]] use $\mathcal C=\mathrm{Open}_X$. There is no need for the objects of $\mathcal C$ to be open sets.
[[Repr|Representable presheaves]] are another basic example.

fields.definition:
The objects of $\mathrm{Pre}(\mathcal C)$ are [[Pshc|presheaves on $\mathcal C$]]. A morphism $\eta:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ is a natural transformation: for each object $U$ there is a map
$$\eta_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U),$$
and for every $u:V\to U$ the square commutes, meaning
$$\mathcal G(u)\circ\eta_U=\eta_V\circ\mathcal F(u).$$
fields.Note: We get the same result whether we first apply $\eta$ and then restrict, or first restrict and then apply $\eta$. Composition and identity morphisms are defined one object at a time.

fields.setting: $\mathcal C$ is locally small, so its morphisms between any two objects form a set. Fix $X\in\mathcal C$.
fields.definition:
The presheaf represented by $X$ is
$$h_X(Y)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Y,X).$$
For $u:Y'\to Y$, restriction is precomposition:
$$h_X(u):h_X(Y)\to h_X(Y'),\qquad g\mapsto g\circ u.$$
A presheaf $\mathcal F$ is representable if it is naturally isomorphic to some $h_X$.
fields.Note: The set $h_X(Y)$ describes $X$ as seen by maps from the test object $Y$. The [[Yond|Yoneda embedding]] says that remembering all these sets and restriction maps retains the morphisms of $\mathcal C$.

fields.statement:
There is a fully faithful functor
$$\mathcal C\longrightarrow\mathrm{Pre}(\mathcal C),\qquad X\longmapsto h_X.$$
A morphism $f:X\to Y$ induces the natural transformation whose component at $T$ sends $g:T\to X$ to $f\circ g:T\to Y$. In particular,
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Pre}(\mathcal C)}(h_X,h_Y).$$
fields.proof:
Given a natural transformation $\eta:h_X\to h_Y$, recover the morphism
$$f=\eta_X(\mathrm{id}_X):X\to Y.$$
Naturality then forces $\eta_T(g)=f\circ g$ for every $g:T\to X$. Thus every natural transformation comes from exactly one morphism.
